content.intro: Learn recursive ctes through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Recursive CTEs matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of recursive ctes is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Anchor and recursive terms, Traversing hierarchical data, Generating sequences where appropriate, Managing recursion termination. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.text: Traversing hierarchical data is a specialized capability whose operators, types, indexes, and compatibility depend on the database engine and installed extensions. Label the target explicitly and provide a portable fallback when the capability is optional.

items.text: Generating sequences where appropriate changes how data is represented or exposed. Check dependencies, name objects consistently, keep structural changes in reviewed migrations, and rehearse the operation against a disposable copy before production.

items.title: Managing recursion termination
items.text: Managing recursion termination summarizes rows. Decide the grain of the result first, group only by the dimensions that define one output row, and verify NULL and duplicate behavior in each metric.

items.title: Preventing infinite recursion
items.text: Preventing infinite recursion helps you structure complex queries with CTEs, recursion, and window functions; choose an approach that keeps logic testable and output rows meaningful. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Recursive query portability
items.text: Recursive query portability helps break a larger query into a precise question. Check the subquery's row count and output columns, account for NULLs in membership tests, and compare the result with a simpler equivalent on a small dataset.

content_blocks.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT employee_id, full_name, manager_id, 0 AS depth
  FROM employees
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.employee_id, e.full_name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1
  FROM employees AS e
  JOIN org AS o ON e.manager_id = o.employee_id
)
SELECT employee_id, full_name, depth
FROM org
ORDER BY depth, employee_id;
content_blocks.expected_output: The query walks the employee hierarchy from manager rows to their reports. The seed schema is acyclic; production recursive queries should handle cycles or enforce a hierarchy rule.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
